column4: The section's disputed reading of ٱسْمَ in 87:1 through the dictionary root و س م becomes literal in سَنَسِمُهُۥ عَلَى ٱلْخُرْطُومِ: the rejecter of recited signs receives an identifying stigma on his nose.
The section's dictionary root و س م appears in الْمُتَوَسِّمِينَ, those who discern signs; the ruined place becomes readable evidence, the inverse use of a brand to identify a person.
The section names أثر as a branch of the root behind تُؤْثِرُونَ; here مِنْ أَثَرِ ٱلسُّجُودِ is the visible trace left by prayer, a good mark set against the brand of disgrace.
Heated gold and silver are pressed against hoarders' foreheads, sides, and backs; the fire-brand is a punishment mark, reversing the section's mark of belonging to the Lord.
Criminals are known بِسِيمَاهُمْ before being seized by forelocks and feet; a visible sign identifies the person for judgment, echoing the snout brand.
The section's brand lexicon says an animal can be recognized by an ear cut or a burn; this ayah names cutting livestock ears as a satanic practice, a reversal of an identifying mark.
Camels are made among God's rites, and His name is spoken over them as they stand; this joins the camel brand scene to a mark of dedication to the true owner.
After the shirt is shown torn from behind, the husband reads that physical trace as proof of the truth; 12:27 supplies the test, making a mark distinguish whose claim is sound.
The torn shirt is used as a diagnostic mark: a tear from behind means Joseph was fleeing, so a bodily trace identifies the action and the truthful speaker.
The youths turn back عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَارِهِمَا, retracing their steps; the section's root ء ث ر includes an iron stamp that makes a camel's footprint recognizable on earth.
The Samiri says he took a handful from أَثَرِ الرَّسُولِ; the same root named in the section makes a remaining trace carry the absent messenger's presence.
The record includes what people send ahead and وَءَاثَارَهُمْ; the section's root gloss of اثر as what remains becomes the deeds' continuing trace.
The command to look at ءَاثَٰرِ رَحْمَتِ ٱللَّهِ makes the revived earth a visible remainder of mercy, an effect that lets a reader recognize its source.
The former peoples left آثارًا فِي الْأَرْضِ, yet greater strength and earthly traces did not save them; the verse gives the section's trace a limit.
This repeated account again speaks of earlier peoples' آثارًا فِي الْأَرْضِ and their end; their impressive marks remain evidence of power, not permanence.
The section's note on the root ع ل م links knowing to a mark that distinguishes; عَلَامَاتٍ here are landmarks that identify a route, with stars also guiding travelers.
The section says what one prefers leaves a trace; here earnings have laid rust over the heart, an inner imprint of a person's acts.
A person makes desire a god, then hearing and heart are sealed and sight covered; the chosen allegiance leaves a mark on the faculties that receive signs.
The section's proposed sense of ٱسْم as a distinguishing mark meets the naming of every thing to Adam; names separate and identify what is otherwise undifferentiated.
أَثَٰرَةٍ مِّنْ عِلْمٍ means a surviving remnant of knowledge demanded as evidence; this is the section's trace-as-remainder idea turned into proof of a claim.
Saqar is described as scorching human skin; the fire leaves a bodily stigma, a negative counterpart to the devotional trace on faces.
The source section names ء ث ر through تُؤْثِرُونَ; سِحْرٌ يُؤْثَرُ here uses that root in the different sense of transmitted magic, the rejecter's dismissal that leads into Saqar at 74:26.
The claim that the rejecter will be cast into Saqar connects the dismissal in 74:24 with a bodily fire mark in 74:29, echoing the section's pairing of rejection and fire.
وَءَاثَرَ الْحَيَوٰةَ الدُّنْيَا uses the same root as the section's تَؤْثِرُونَ for preferring worldly life; this is its most direct parallel for a choice that leaves a recognizable trace.
لَن نُّؤْثِرَكَ uses the section's root ء ث ر in the opposite choice: the magicians will not prefer Pharaoh over clear proofs, choosing the Lord's sign over worldly coercion.
Allah owns the most beautiful names and is invoked by them; the command to leave those who distort His names parallels the section's call to keep the Lord's identifying name free of flaw.
Allah's beautiful names belong to the Creator and Fashioner, and all creation glorifies Him; the owner-name relation gives substance to the section's expanded reading of tasbih.
Prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are declared for Allah, Lord of the worlds; this makes the section's owner-mark concrete as a whole life identified with its Lord.
The verse says to eat what has Allah's name mentioned over it; spoken naming marks the animal as dedicated to its true owner.
The inverse boundary is explicit: an animal without Allah's name mentioned over it is not to be eaten, and the verse associates that omission with disobedience and satanic prompting.
Each community has rites in which God's name is mentioned over the livestock He provides; the name marks whose provision and offering the animal is.
Houses are raised for Allah's name to be remembered and glorified morning and evening; this places the Lord's name in a visible devotional setting, like an affiliation mark.
Commerce does not distract these men from God's remembrance and prayer; their priorities make the name-bearing community recognizable against the world's pull.
Those who call on their Lord morning and evening seek His face; the Prophet is told not to turn away toward worldly adornment, joining remembrance with a refusal of status marks.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from remembrance of Allah; doing so marks the losing side of the section's choice.
Family, wealth, trade, and homes become a boundary when they are dearer than Allah and His Messenger; the verse makes worldly preference a public allegiance.
Meat and blood do not reach God, only taqwa; this limits the camel and name rite outward sign to inward devotion rather than a physical brand alone.
The brothers display Joseph's shirt with false blood; a fabricated trace can mislead, so the section's act of reading signs requires discernment.
The overturned town and rain of stones are the physical remainder behind 15:75's signs for discerners; the ruin itself supplies what the reader inspects.
After Lot's town is destroyed, a clear sign is left from it for people who reason; like 15:75, the ruined place bears a readable trace of judgment.
The empty houses of former wrongdoers are called a sign for those who know; built places become residual marks by which a people are recognized.
Hearing, sight, and skins testify to what people did; the body preserves evidence of action, turning a mark into testimony.
The skins answer that Allah made them speak; this completes 41:20's bodily testimony and shows that the trace cannot be concealed from its owner.
Tongues, hands, and feet testify to what people did; bodily traces identify the actions behind a person's outward appearance.
With mouths sealed, hands speak and feet testify to what people earned; the body becomes an indelible record of the choices that marked it.
On the quake day the earth reports its news; the ground itself retains and reveals traces of what happened on it.
The next ayah says the earth reports because its Lord inspired it, completing 99:4's image of the ground as a witness to its traces.
The ruined place lies on an established road; after 15:75 calls it a sign for discerners, this ayah makes the mark something travelers continue to encounter.
People on the heights recognize each group by its marks; 7:48 continues their address to those recognized, a direct scene of identity read from signs.
The men of the heights call people they recognize by their marks; the dialogue completes 7:46's image of a sign distinguishing persons.
Restrained poor people are recognized by their marks even though they do not beg; this is a compassionate, positive counterpart to a punitive brand.
The hypocrites would be known by their marks and by the tone of their speech; hidden allegiance becomes legible through outward signs and words.
Faces become white or black on the Day of Judgment, publicly separating groups; the face carries a moral sign, unlike the single mark of prostration.
Evil-doers' faces are covered with patches like night and humiliation; the visible stain reverses the good trace of prostration.
صبغة الله, God's dye, gives the believers a marked identity; it is a specific metaphor for belonging, though not the section's proposed root for ٱسْم.
The verse denies that God instituted the named classes of marked livestock; it sets a boundary against invented ownership signs and animal categories.
People assign portions of crops and cattle to God and partners, then misdirect them; this exposes false claims of ownership against the section's true Lord.
Saqar leaves nothing and spares nothing; beside the section's trace-as-remainder, this is a specific reversal where destructive fire erases rather than leaves a mark.
Everything on earth perishes; the section's trace and preference theme is set against what can vanish.
The face of the Lord remains; this names the enduring owner behind the section's contrast between the passing world and the Lord's mark.
What people possess will end, while what is with Allah remains; this directly develops أثر as remainder and the section's worldly/lasting contrast.
Wealth and children are adornment of worldly life, while الباقيات الصالحات are better and lasting; the enduring deeds are a good trace after worldly marks fade.
Worldly gifts are enjoyment and adornment, while what is with Allah is better and more lasting; this states the precise passing/remaining relation behind the section's gloss.
The same worldly-enjoyment versus better, lasting provision with Allah is restated for believers; it makes the section's mark of preference consequential.
The Prophet is told not to fix his eyes on worldly splendor, since his Lord's provision is better and more lasting; this turns preference into a visible discipline of attention.
The Hereafter is better than the first life; this is the section's contrast between the preferred near life and what endures.
This life's play and amusement is bounded by the better home of the Hereafter for the God-fearing; it parallels the choice that reveals allegiance.
This life is amusement, while the Hereafter is the true life; the contrast gives weight to the section's trace of what remains.
The worldly life is pictured as rain-fed growth that yellows and becomes debris; the scene meets 87:4-5's pasture turned dark stubble and exposes the passing world.
بَلْ تُحِبُّونَ الْعَاجِلَةَ states love of the immediate life, the same preference identified in 87:16.
وَتَذَرُونَ الْآخِرَةَ supplies the other half of 75:20's choice; it completes the section's contrast with the life that remains.
They love the immediate life and leave a heavy day behind; the verse makes the preference's neglected aftermath explicit.
Whoever wants the immediate life is given what God wills, then faces blame and Hell; the choice leaves a consequence, as in the section's fire-mark contrast.
Whoever wants the Hereafter and strives as a believer has effort acknowledged; this is the opposite trace to the worldly preference of 87:16.
The refuge of the one who preferred worldly life is Hell; the neighboring verse makes the section's pairing of choice and fire explicit.
The one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains desire is the reversal of the one who prefers the world, matching the section's two marks.
The refuge for that restrained person is the Garden, completing the boundary opposite the Hell in 79:39.
The disbelievers are described as having preferred worldly life over the Hereafter; the same priority leaves a defining allegiance.
Those who love worldly life over the Hereafter and obstruct God's path embody the preference whose trace identifies a person.
The challenge asks whether people are content with this life instead of the Hereafter, whose enjoyment is small; it gives the preference a clear limit.
Believers are urged to sell the present life for the Hereafter; this reverses the section's preference and makes allegiance visible in a choice.
At Uhud, some wanted the world and some the Hereafter; the split in preference had a consequence in the battle, giving the choice a concrete mark.
The Prophet is told to turn from one who turns away from the Reminder and desires only worldly life; this joins neglected remembrance to the section's defining preference.
The magicians say they believe in their Lord and that Allah is better and more lasting; this completes 20:72's refusal to prefer Pharaoh and the worldly power he commands.
This life is only temporary enjoyment, while the Hereafter is the abiding home; it restates the trace's passing/remaining boundary.
The trained hunting animal catches prey, and Allah's name is mentioned over the catch; this is another specific case where the name marks an animal as lawfully dedicated to its Lord.
When believers are reminded of God's signs, they fall in prostration and glorify Him without arrogance; this joins the section's name-and-prayer mark to the act that leaves أثر السجود in 48:29.
Allah knows every fallen leaf and every seed hidden in the earth; the root ع ل م from the section meets its concern with visible and hidden traces in a specific scene of plant remains.
Following 16:107's statement that they preferred worldly life, this ayah says their hearts, hearing, and sight are sealed; the preference leaves a spiritual mark.
Those content with worldly life and heedless of God's signs are the reverse of the one who fears and remembers; this joins the section's preference and sign themes.
The next ayah gives those heedless people the Fire as their abode for what they earned, completing 10:7's choice of worldly life with the section's fire-mark.
People who want worldly life and its adornment are a direct counterpart to those who prefer it in 87:16; their aim exposes what they prize.
The next ayah says such people have no share in the Hereafter, their work is nullified, and they meet the Fire; it makes the passing choice's consequence explicit.
The treasure beneath the wall is preserved for two orphans because their father was righteous; a parent's virtue leaves a concrete hidden remainder for those who come after.
The world's life is likened to rain-fed growth that becomes dry stubble scattered by wind; the plant's remaining debris meets the section's trace-as-remainder and worldly-life contrast.
The worldly life is compared to vegetation that flourishes, then becomes harvest debris; this is another direct rendering of growth passing into a trace.
The crops grow in varied colors, yellow, then become debris; this repeated plant cycle makes the remnant after flourishing visible.
People know only the outward surface of worldly life and are heedless of the Hereafter; this contrasts their limited knowing with Allah's knowledge of public and hidden things in the section.
Joseph says the supposed gods are only names people assigned, with no authority, while judgment belongs to Allah; this bounds the section's disputed reading of name as a mark of true ownership.
The idols are called names invented by people without divine authority; the ayah distinguishes a label from the Lord who truly owns and judges.
Hud challenges the people over names they and their fathers assigned without God's authority; the section's name-as-mark reading meets a boundary where naming cannot establish rightful ownership.
This ayah continues 6:118 by asking why people would not eat what has Allah's name mentioned over it and clarifying the exception; it spells out the boundary conveyed by naming the offering.

The list of worldly attractions includes wealth, livestock, and fields, all described as enjoyment of near life while the good return is with Allah; it gives concrete objects one may prefer over what remains.
Those who buy worldly life in exchange for the Hereafter face unlightened punishment; this is another direct statement of a choice that marks the person for an outcome.
One who desires the Hereafter's harvest has it increased, while one who desires this world's harvest receives only it and has no share in the Hereafter; the preference's result is made explicit.
All things perish except the face of the Lord; this repeats the section's contrast between what passes and the enduring Lord behind the identifying mark.
The righteous are given a sealed drink, the object whose khitām is described in 83:26; if khitām means a seal, this offers a good mark opposite the stigma of the brand.
خِتَامُهُ مِسْكٌ may mean the drink's seal or its finishing taste; on the seal reading, musk identifies the righteous drink and reverses the fire brand, while the taste reading is a weaker parallel.
